differentialModel.answer: Childhood nephrotic syndrome, first episode, no atypical features. Consider acute glomerulonephritis with a nephritic picture, and protein energy malnutrition with liver disease as the non-renal mimics.

diagnosis.answer: Nephrotic syndrome, first episode, with heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and hyperlipidaemia, normal blood pressure and no haematuria.

skill.exam.paed.cvs.pulses_bp.finding: Blood pressure 94/58, normal for age and height on repeat measurement with a paediatric cuff. Femoral pulses felt, no radiofemoral delay.

skill.exam.paed.gi.ascites.finding: Flanks full with shifting dullness on turning to the side. Mild fluid thrill. No tenderness, no guarding.

skill.exam.paed.gi.inspection.finding: Belly uniformly swollen with shiny skin and an everted umbilicus. Scrotal swelling present, skin intact, testes palpable. No dilated veins, no jaundice.

skill.exam.paed.gi.palpation_percussion.finding: Belly soft, liver edge felt two fingers below the costal margin, pushed down and non-tender. Spleen not felt. Kidneys not ballotable. No lump.

skill.exam.paed.weight.finding: Weight 18 kg today against a recorded 16 kg a month ago at the anganwadi. Height 102 cm. Weight gain with a poor appetite means retained fluid.

skill.gen.paed.appearance.finding: Alert and playful 4-year-old with marked puffiness of the face and eyelids, pitting swelling of the feet and legs, and a swollen belly. No distress, no pallor of note, no breathlessness at rest.

skill.gen.paed.edema.finding: Soft pitting oedema over the eyelids, shins and feet. A pit held for five seconds over the shin stays visible. Worst around the eyes in the morning by the mother's account.

skill.gen.paed.pallor.finding: No severe pallor of the conjunctiva, tongue or palms.

skill.gen.paed.vitals.finding: Temperature 37.1 C. Heart rate 108 regular. Respiratory rate 24. SpO2 98 percent on room air. Blood pressure normal as above.

cases.fallback: I am not sure what you mean, doctor. Can you ask that a different way?

appetite_weight.reply: He eats less than before, yet his clothes have gone tight and he feels heavier when I lift him. The anganwadi weighing showed a clear gain.

belly_pain.reply: No belly pain and no fever. He plays as usual, only slower because of the swelling.

breathlessness.reply: No breathlessness and no cough. He runs a little and then sits, but his breathing stays easy.

comorbidity.reply: No past admissions and no long illness. He had the usual colds, nothing with swelling before this.

drugs.reply: No medicines except a fever syrup once. Nobody has given steroids or water tablets.

family.reply: No kidney trouble in the family. My husband and I are not related by blood, and there is no deafness at home.

fever.reply: No fever through this illness. Two weeks before the puffiness he had a running nose and mild fever for three days, which settled on its own.

immunisation.reply: He had all the government injections up to his age, sister. I do not think he had any special pneumonia injection.

oedema_course.reply: The eyes first, three weeks ago. Then the feet by evening, and now the whole body including the belly. Mornings the face is worst, evenings the feet.

oedema_pitting.reply: It is soft. When I press his leg with my thumb the dent stays for a while.

past_episodes.reply: Never before. This is the first time his face has swollen like this.

presenting.reply: Doctor, my son Aarav's face has been puffy for three weeks, and now his feet and belly are swollen too. His urine looks frothy.

salt_diet.reply: He eats roti, dal, rice and vegetables with us. He likes papad and pickle with food. Milk once a day.

sore_throat_skin.reply: No sore throat, no skin boils, and the urine is pale and frothy, never dark or red.

trigger.reply: Only that running nose two weeks before the puffiness. No new food, no new medicine, no insect bite.

urine.reply: The urine froths like soap water and he passes less than before, though he goes without burning. No bedwetting.

complement.note: Not indicated first line here: no haematuria, normal pressure and preserved function. Reserved for nephritic or atypical features.

fbc.note: Baseline before steroids, and anaemia would need its own explanation.
fbc.result: Haemoglobin normal for age. Counts unremarkable.

upcr.result: Raised in the nephrotic range, matching the dipstick protein.

urine.note: The single test that must never be skipped in a swollen child.
urine.result: Protein strongly positive on dipstick. No red cells seen. No pus cells.

managementModel.answer: Confirm the workup, start an empirical oral corticosteroid course per guideline with family counselling on relapse, advise salt restriction with judicious diuretics only, review pneumococcal and scheduled vaccines, teach home dipstick and daily weights, and watch for infection and thrombosis.

teachingPoints: The sequence tells the diagnosis: periorbital puffiness on waking spreading to dependent parts over weeks, with frothy urine, is nephrotic until proven otherwise.
Normal pressure with no haematuria keeps this case typical and steroid-first. Either finding in the opposite direction would reframe it as nephritic or atypical.
The urine test is the hinge of the whole case. Swelling without proteinuria is a different disease list.
Weight gain with poor appetite means fluid, and serial weights with dipsticks become the family's monitoring tools.
Fever with belly pain or a painful swollen limb after this visit would mean infection of the fluid or a clot, not a routine relapse.
Missing pneumococcal vaccine in a nephrotic child is a prevention gap to close at the first visit, not during a febrile crisis.

skill.reasoning.nephrotic.basics.body: Nephrotic syndrome is a pattern of findings caused by heavy leakage of protein through the kidney filters, not a single disease. Four findings travel together: large amounts of protein in the urine, low albumin in the blood, swelling of the body, and raised blood fats.
keyPoints: The four linked findings are heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and hyperlipidaemia. Each follows from the protein leak, so finding one should prompt a search for the other three.

In children the cause is most often idiopathic, with no systemic disease behind it. The commonest tissue pattern in young children is minimal change disease, in which the filters look almost normal under the light microscope.
Swelling is the usual presenting feature. It typically starts around the eyes on waking and becomes generalised with dependent swelling, sometimes with fluid in the belly.
Most childhood cases respond to corticosteroids, so a trial of steroids is the standard first step in the typical age group, without an initial kidney biopsy.
A biopsy is reserved for atypical features: onset outside the usual age range, visible blood in the urine, raised blood pressure, impaired kidney function, or failure to respond to steroids.
Relapses are common. The pattern of response over time classifies the disease as steroid-sensitive, frequently relapsing, steroid-dependent, or steroid-resistant, and each pattern has its own plan.
skill.reasoning.nephrotic.basics.oneLine: Four linked findings from a leaky kidney filter, usually steroid-sensitive
pitfalls: Calling any swollen child nephrotic without testing the urine for protein.
Ordering a biopsy in a typical preschool child before trying steroids.
Forgetting that the disease is defined by the four findings together, not by swelling alone.

probes.a: Heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, and hyperlipidaemia.
probes.q: Name the four findings that define the nephrotic syndrome.

probes.a: Minimal change disease, which is why most preschool children respond to steroids without a biopsy.
probes.q: What is the commonest histology in young children, and what follows from it?

probes.a: Atypical age, gross haematuria, hypertension, impaired renal function, or steroid resistance.
probes.q: When is a renal biopsy indicated rather than an empirical steroid trial?

skill.reasoning.nephrotic.basics.title: What nephrotic syndrome is
skill.reasoning.nephrotic.basics.why: The student who holds the four findings and their single shared cause can recognise the syndrome from the doorway, while the student who memorises swelling alone will confuse it with cardiac, liver and nutritional oedema.

skill.reasoning.nephrotic.findings.body: Lost protein explains the whole bedside picture. Albumin leaking into the urine lowers the protein level in the blood, fluid leaves the vessels for the tissues, and the liver compensates by making extra fats. Every sign you elicited traces back to that leak.
keyPoints: Oedema is soft, pitting and generalised, worst around the eyes in the morning and over the feet and shins by evening. In anasarca the whole body is swollen, including the genitalia, with fluid in the belly and sometimes around the lungs.
The child usually looks well nourished despite the swelling, with normal pressure and no distress. Wasting, severe pallor or breathlessness at rest argue for another cause or a complication.
Ascites gives a uniformly distended belly with full flanks, shifting dullness and a fluid thrill when tense. The liver edge may be felt, pushed down by fluid rather than enlarged by disease.
Blood pressure is typically normal. A raised pressure, visible blood in the urine, or a raised creatinine marks the case as atypical and pushes the workup towards nephritic and secondary causes.
Daily weight is the truest measure of the oedema. A rising weight with a falling urine output means fluid is accumulating; a brisk fall in weight on treatment means the diuresis has begun.

Two complications hide behind the swelling. Fever with a tender belly means infection of the fluid until proven otherwise, and a swollen painful limb, chest pain or breathlessness means a clot until proven otherwise.
skill.reasoning.nephrotic.findings.oneLine: One leak explains the swelling, the fluid, the fats and the risks
pitfalls: Calling the pushed-down liver edge hepatomegaly and working up liver disease.
Recording oedema without daily weights, so response to treatment cannot be judged.
Missing the tender belly with fever or the painful swollen limb while admiring the classic picture.

probes.a: Soft pitting oedema worst around the eyes in the morning, becoming generalised, with ascites in severe cases.
probes.q: Describe the characteristic distribution of nephrotic oedema.

probes.a: No, it is usually normal, and a raised pressure marks the case as atypical and changes the workup.
probes.q: Is hypertension expected in uncomplicated nephrotic syndrome?

probes.a: Fever with a tender belly suggests infection of ascitic fluid, and a painful swollen limb suggests thrombosis.
probes.q: Which two complications must be excluded in a febrile oedematous child with belly pain?

skill.reasoning.nephrotic.findings.title: The nephrotic picture
skill.reasoning.nephrotic.findings.why: A single mechanism, protein leaking through injured filters, generates the swelling, the fluid, the blood results and the two dangerous complications, and seeing that unity stops the findings being memorised as a list.

skill.reasoning.nephrotic.summary.body: State the child with the age clue, the tempo, the syndrome in abstract terms, and the response pattern, in that order.
keyPoints: Name the child with the age clue: a preschool child with a first episode carries a different probability from an infant or an adolescent with relapsing disease.
State the tempo: swelling that built over days to weeks, with the morning-evening rhythm and the urine findings alongside.
State the syndrome in abstract terms: generalised pitting oedema with heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and hyperlipidaemia, with or without ascites.
Include the atypical markers or their absence: blood pressure, visible haematuria, and renal function, since these decide biopsy and referral in the same sentence.
Close with the response pattern where known: first episode, steroid-sensitive, frequently relapsing, steroid-dependent, or steroid-resistant.

A worked example: A 4-year-old boy presents with three weeks of periorbital puffiness progressing to generalised pitting oedema with ascites and frothy urine. Blood pressure is normal, there is no haematuria, and renal function is preserved. This is nephrotic syndrome, first episode, with no atypical features.
skill.reasoning.nephrotic.summary.oneLine: Problem representation for a relapsing swelling illness
pitfalls: Omitting the age clue, so the listener cannot judge the probability of steroid sensitivity.
Leaving out blood pressure and haematuria, the two negatives doing the most work.
Ending without the response pattern, which is what the next plan depends on.

probes.a: The response pattern, such as first episode or frequently relapsing, because it directly determines the next plan.
probes.q: What element belongs in a nephrotic summary that a pneumonia summary does not need?

probes.a: Blood pressure and visible haematuria, whose absence keeps the case in the typical steroid-sensitive group.
probes.q: Which two negatives must every nephrotic summary carry, and why?

rubric.text: States the child with the age clue
States the tempo as days to weeks with the diurnal rhythm
Includes blood pressure, haematuria and renal function or their absence

skill.reasoning.nephrotic.summary.title: The clinical summary
skill.reasoning.nephrotic.summary.why: The summary of a relapsing illness must carry the response pattern alongside the syndrome, because the pattern, not the swelling, decides whether this child needs steroids alone or referral.

skill.investigation.nephrotic.workup.body: Group investigations by what they answer: prove the protein loss, show its consequences, check kidney function, and exclude the mimics that need a different plan.
keyPoints: PROVE THE LEAK: urine routine and microscopy for protein and red cells, with quantification of proteinuria by a spot urine protein to creatinine ratio or a timed collection, plus home dipstick testing that later becomes the relapse monitor.
SHOW THE CONSEQUENCES: serum albumin and total protein, which fall, and a lipid profile, which rises. These complete the four findings and need no biopsy to interpret.
CHECK KIDNEY FUNCTION: renal function and electrolytes, and a full blood count. Function is usually preserved in uncomplicated disease, and a raised creatinine marks the case as atypical.
EXCLUDE THE MIMICS: complement levels and autoimmune serology when there is haematuria, hypertension or impaired function, pointing towards nephritic and lupus disease.
RESERVE THE INVASIVE TEST: renal biopsy for atypical features or steroid resistance, arranged through paediatric nephrology, not as a first step in a typical preschool child.
Track response with daily weight, urine output, dipstick protein, blood pressure and growth. These five bedside measures matter more than repeated blood tests once treatment starts.
skill.investigation.nephrotic.workup.oneLine: Prove the leak, show its cost, exclude the mimics
pitfalls: Starting steroids without a baseline urine protein quantification, so response can never be measured.
Biopsying a typical preschool child before a steroid trial.
Repeating blood tests while ignoring daily weight, dipstick and blood pressure, the measures that actually steer care.

probes.a: Urine protein quantification with a protein to creatinine ratio or timed collection, alongside dipstick testing.
probes.q: What urine test quantifies the protein leak?

probes.a: Low albumin and total protein with raised lipids, completing the nephrotic pattern.
probes.q: What blood results do you expect alongside heavy proteinuria?

probes.a: Haematuria with hypertension or impaired function, prompting complement and autoimmune serology and referral for biopsy.
probes.q: When do you extend the workup beyond albumin, lipids and renal function?

skill.investigation.nephrotic.workup.title: Confirming and grading the illness
skill.investigation.nephrotic.workup.why: Investigations here have four separate jobs, and knowing which test does which stops the student biopsying a typical child or missing the complement result that reframes the case.

skill.reasoning.nephrotic.diagnosis.body: The diagnosis is made on the four findings with normal pressure and preserved function, and it is completed by the response pattern over time. Typical disease needs no biopsy; atypical disease needs referral.
keyPoints: Diagnose nephrotic syndrome when heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia travel together in a child with normal blood pressure and no gross haematuria.

Mark the case as atypical when any of these appear: onset in infancy or adolescence, visible blood in the urine, raised blood pressure, impaired renal function, or low complement. Atypical cases need paediatric nephrology review and usually a biopsy.

Classify by response once steroids are given: steroid-sensitive disease remits on steroids; frequently relapsing disease returns repeatedly; steroid-dependent disease returns as steroids are tapered; steroid-resistant disease never remits and needs biopsy.
A complete diagnostic statement names the syndrome, the episode, the atypical markers or their absence, and the response pattern: nephrotic syndrome, first episode, no atypical features.

Steroid-sensitive minimal change disease carries a good long-term kidney outlook despite repeated relapses. Steroid resistance, often from focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, carries a higher risk of progression to chronic kidney disease.
skill.reasoning.nephrotic.diagnosis.oneLine: Four findings name it, atypical markers grade it, response classifies it
pitfalls: Calling the diagnosis from swelling and albumin alone without quantifying proteinuria.
Labelling steroid resistance before an adequate steroid course has been given and supervised.
Giving every relapse the same label instead of tracking the pattern that decides steroid-sparing treatment.

probes.a: Heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia, with normal pressure and no gross haematuria.
probes.q: What combination of findings makes the diagnosis of nephrotic syndrome?

probes.a: Infantile or adolescent onset, haematuria, hypertension, impaired function, or low complement, needing nephrology referral and usually biopsy.
probes.q: Name three atypical features and what they trigger.

probes.a: Frequently relapsing, steroid-dependent, or steroid-resistant disease, each with its own plan including steroid-sparing agents and biopsy.
probes.q: How is the disease classified by its response to steroids?

rubric.text: States the four findings that make the diagnosis
Checks and states the atypical markers

skill.reasoning.nephrotic.diagnosis.title: Diagnosis and response pattern
skill.reasoning.nephrotic.diagnosis.why: The name alone does not say whether this child goes home on steroids or to a nephrology centre for biopsy, and the response pattern is the classifier that decides it.

skill.reasoning.nephrotic.differential.body: For a swollen child with protein in the urine, exclude nephritic disease first, then inherited and secondary kidney causes, then non-renal oedema.
keyPoints: Acute glomerulonephritis with a nephritic picture: favoured by cola-coloured urine, raised blood pressure, and impaired renal function after a sore throat or skin sores. This is the first mimic to exclude, because its management differs completely.

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis: favoured by steroid resistance, older age at onset, and persistent heavy proteinuria. It is the usual explanation when steroids fail, and it needs biopsy and nephrology care.
Membranous nephropathy: uncommon in children, considered in adolescents and in secondary settings rather than in a typical preschool child.
Henoch Schonlein purpura nephritis: favoured by a purpuric rash over the buttocks and legs with joint and belly pain alongside the urine findings.
Lupus nephritis: favoured by fever, rash, joint pains and positive autoimmune serology, particularly in an older girl.
Congenital nephrotic syndrome: presents in the first year of life, often with a family history and consanguinity, and needs referral rather than repeated steroid courses.

Non-renal oedema: cardiac, liver and nutritional causes. Favoured by breathlessness with a gallop, jaundice with a firm liver, or wasting with classic skin and hair changes, each with little or no proteinuria.
skill.reasoning.nephrotic.differential.oneLine: Nephritic first, inherited and secondary next, non-renal last
pitfalls: Treating a nephritic child with an empirical steroid course meant for nephrotic disease.
Repeating steroids for resistant disease without considering focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and biopsy.
Forgetting nutritional and liver oedema in a wasted child, where proteinuria is absent.

probes.a: Acute glomerulonephritis, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis, Henoch Schonlein purpura nephritis, lupus nephritis, congenital nephrotic syndrome, and non-renal oedema.
probes.q: Name four differentials for a swollen child with proteinuria.

probes.a: Cola-coloured urine with hypertension and impaired function after streptococcal infection, managed as nephritic disease rather than with empirical steroids.
probes.q: How do you distinguish a nephritic mimic at the bedside?

rubric.text: Spans nephritic, glomerular, systemic and non-renal causes
States when resistant or atypical disease needs biopsy

skill.reasoning.nephrotic.differential.title: Differential diagnosis
skill.reasoning.nephrotic.differential.why: Most puffy preschool children are exactly what they look like, but the nephritic, inherited and secondary cases hiding among them need entirely different care, and the differential is what catches them.

skill.treatment.nephrotic.care.body: Treat the protein leak first with steroids, support the child through salt sense and careful fluid handling, and guard throughout against the two great complications: infection and clotting.
skill.treatment.nephrotic.care.dosingNote: This module teaches management at the level of drug CLASS and principle. Specific agents, doses, schedules and durations must be taken from your current national or institutional guideline, such as the Indian Academy of Pediatrics guidance, and the paediatric nephrologist's prescription at the time of treatment. CliniX does not prescribe.
keyPoints: First-line definitive therapy is an empirical course of oral corticosteroids, which brings remission in most children with steroid-sensitive minimal change disease. The exact schedule is set by the treating guideline and the nephrologist, not memorised here.

Manage frequently relapsing or steroid-dependent disease with steroid-sparing agents such as levamisole, a calcineurin inhibitor such as ciclosporin or tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, or rituximab, chosen with paediatric nephrology.

Control oedema with sensible dietary salt restriction and judicious loop diuretics, avoiding aggressive diuresis that precipitates hypovolaemia and thrombosis. Cautious albumin infusion is reserved for severe symptomatic oedema with circulatory compromise.

Reduce infection risk through pneumococcal and other scheduled vaccination, and treat fever with belly pain as suspected infection of the ascitic fluid until proven otherwise. Review the immunisation card at the first visit, since nephrotic syndrome places the child in the high-risk vaccine group.
Mitigate the hypercoagulable state with mobilisation, avoidance of prolonged bed rest and dehydration, and thromboprophylaxis in high-risk children as advised by the treating team.

Monitor with home urine dipstick testing to catch relapse early, alongside surveillance of blood pressure, weight, growth, urine output, and corticosteroid effects such as appetite change, weight gain and behaviour change.

Refer for renal biopsy and paediatric nephrology input in atypical or steroid-resistant disease, often focal segmental glomerulosclerosis. In the Indian setting this means timely referral to the district medical college or a paediatric nephrology centre, with shared follow-up closer home.

Counsel the family from day one: relapses are common and expected, daily weights and dipsticks are their tools, salt sense continues between episodes, and the child should return promptly with fever and belly pain, swelling of one limb, breathlessness, or sharply reduced urine.
skill.treatment.nephrotic.care.oneLine: Steroids for the leak, sense for the salt, vigilance for infection and clots
pitfalls: Prescribing steroid doses and tapers from memory instead of the current guideline and the nephrologist's chart.
Diuresing aggressively and precipitating hypovolaemia and thrombosis in an intravascularly depleted child.
Discharging a relapsing child without home dipsticks, a written relapse plan, and vaccine review.
Missing atypical or resistant disease and repeating steroid courses instead of referring for biopsy.

probes.a: An empirical course of oral corticosteroids, which induces remission in most steroid-sensitive cases.
probes.q: What is the first-line definitive therapy for typical childhood nephrotic syndrome?

probes.a: Levamisole, a calcineurin inhibitor, mycophenolate mofetil or rituximab, with paediatric nephrology.
probes.q: Name two steroid-sparing options for relapsing disease.

probes.a: Home urine dipstick monitoring with blood pressure, weight, growth and steroid-effect surveillance.
probes.q: How is a child on treatment monitored between visits?

skill.treatment.nephrotic.care.title: Managing nephrotic syndrome
skill.treatment.nephrotic.care.why: The steroid course decides the outcome, but the salt advice, the dipsticks, the vaccines and the vigilance for infection and clots decide whether the child survives the illness unharmed, and each of these is grounded in the knowledge base.
